subject: bicycle
reasoning:
I'm planning out a vintage bicycle build using the SDK, mapping out the joints, parts, and rod connections I'll need to construct the frame, wheels, and other components with correct API usage.

For the design itself, I'm picturing a 1930s roadster-style bicycle: large ~26" wheels, a wheelbase around 1.05m, classic tube frame (top, down, seat tube, stays), upright handlebars, a leather saddle, chainring and crank, cream tires with black sidewalls, big stylistic fenders, and charming details like a front wicker basket, bell, and headlamp, all finished in a deep racing green frame color.

Now I'm working out the geometry: setting up the coordinate system with the bike facing +Z and ground at y=0, then calculating wheel radius, hub heights, wheelbase spacing, and bottom bracket position, followed by computing the seat tube and head tube angles and placement using trigonometry to get realistic vintage frame geometry.

Continuing those calculations, I'm positioning the head tube top and bottom points using the 70° head angle, then figuring out the fork's path from the head tube down to the front hub, and finally working out the top tube, down tube, seat stays, and chainstays connecting all the major frame points together.

For the dropouts and stays, I'm offsetting the rear axle points to either side of center at x=±0.06 for a proper dual-sided frame, using tapered rods for the chainstays. For coloring, I'm settling on a deep racing green for the main tubes with cream pinstriping, considering whether to implement the stripe as a coordinate-based paint function along the top tube or keep things simpler with solid colors and separate badge details.

I'm deciding to keep the tubes solid green rather than add pinstripe rods, and instead focus visual interest on a front wicker basket—building it as a lathe-shaped bowl with a woven-looking stripe paint pattern along the y-axis—plus a leather saddle with a mottled brown texture. For the wheels, I'm constructing the rims as chrome tori rotated so their axis aligns with the X-axis for the axle.

Writing wheel assembly code...

Setting thetaStart=0 and thetaLength=π gives the correct top-half coverage with outward-facing normals, positioned at radius 0.37 just outside the tire. I'll keep most parts as simple colored meshes but consider adding richer paint materials for the basket and saddle for visual variety. Fenders should stay attached to the frame rather than the wheel bones, though the front fender needs to track the fork/steering joint rather than the static frame.

I'm now sketching the joint hierarchy: a root "frame" joint near the bottom bracket, a "fork" child joint at the head tube for steering, "wheelF" and "wheelR" children for the front and rear wheels, a "crank" joint for the pedals, a "bars" joint on the fork for handlebars, and a "saddle" joint off the frame. I'm reasoning through joint directions and rotation axes, deciding not to overcomplicate it since default orientation inherits from the parent when no explicit direction is given.

Now I'm working out geometry for the crank arms, chainring, and pedals—placing the crank arms at offset positions along the bottom bracket axle, sizing the chainring and orienting it to face sideways, and thinking about whether to add a simple chain connecting the chainring to the rear sprocket or skip it for simplicity.

For the saddle, I'm deciding to build it as a swept shape along a curved path running from the back to the front, using an elliptical cross-section that tapers in width to mimic a saddle's profile, attached to the frame at the seat tube.

For the handlebars I'm using a curved sweep through several waypoints mimicking a typical bar shape, with thicker grip ends in black, and the pedals as simple small black boxes attached at the crank ends. For the front fender I'm planning a half-cylinder shape sized slightly larger than the wheel radius, centered on the front hub and attached near the fork joint.

For the rear fender I'll do a similar half-cylinder mounted on the frame at the rear hub position, and I'm thinking through where to place a vintage-style front basket -- positioning it above and in front of the handlebars using a lathed bowl shape with a narrower base and wider top, mounted via a rack rod to the fork so it doesn't rotate with steering.

I'm defining the basket's wicker-like texture using horizontal stripe bands along the y-axis, and working out the lathe profile points so the outline closes properly along the axis for a smooth bowl shape.

Now I'm placing the basket on the fork, adjusting its height so it sits lower under the handlebars without colliding with the front wheel or fender, then adding a thin chrome rod connecting the fork crown to the basket bottom as a support rack. I'm also planning a small brass bell near the handlebars and a headlamp fixture at the front.

I'm deciding to skip the headlamp since it clashes with the basket, keeping just the bell, and adding small sphere lugs at joints like the head tube, bottom bracket, and rear dropouts for a decorative frame detail. I'm now specifying the tube radii for the top tube, down tube, seat tube, and head tube, along with rod dimensions for the fork legs and crown, planning to attach each frame piece explicitly to the frame bone.

I'm setting up the joint hierarchy, starting with the root frame joint and explicitly defining parent-child relationships so each joint like the fork and front wheel inherits proper positioning and rotation along the steering axis.

For attachment, I'll use the fork bone directly for steering-related parts like the bars rather than creating a separate joint, keeping the fender and other frame-mounted parts tied to the main frame bone. I'm skipping roles since they don't apply well here, and now thinking about which paint finishes to apply—considering mottled leather for the saddle, wicker texture for the basket, and possibly a lacquer-style paint for the fenders.

Trying out a pinstripe effect for the fender using an angular paint function around the axis turned out messy, so I'm abandoning that in favor of solid color enamel finishes, reserving mottle for the leather saddle and wicker paint for the basket, with chrome for spokes and brass for the bell instead.

Writing bicycle component code...

I'm computing hub and rim positions for the spokes using polar coordinates in the YZ plane, then placing 20 radial rods per wheel as thin chrome rods bonded to the wheel joint, keeping triangle and part counts well within limits. For the wheel itself, I'm layering a chrome rim torus and a cream tire torus, both rotated so their axis aligns with the wheel's X-axis, and attaching them to the hub joint for proper positioning.

I'm defining the hub as a small chrome cylinder rotated to align with the axle, then adding an open half-cylinder fender over each wheel sized to just clear the tire radius, carefully working out the rotation math so the fender's circular cross-section sits correctly in the YZ plane and the opening faces the right direction.

Now I'm positioning the rear and front wheel hubs, verifying the tire sinks only slightly into the ground, then mapping out the chainstay and seat stay rod endpoints so they connect the bottom bracket and seat tube to the rear dropouts at the correct hub width.

I'm computing exact 3D coordinates for the top tube, down tube, head tube, and seat tube between the bottom bracket, head tube, and saddle region, then planning the fork crown and legs connecting to the front hub. I'm adding small lug spheres at the BB and head tube joints, defining the seatpost and saddle as a tapered catmull-rom sweep with leather mottle paint, then laying out the crankset: chainring position, crank arms on either side of the BB, pedal boxes, and a chain connecting chainring to rear sprocket with horizontal top and angled bottom runs.

I'm positioning handlebars as a symmetric catmull curve stemming from the head tube, adding grips at the bar ends, a small bell, a front basket mounted via rack rods above the fender with contrasting stripe paint, and a brass headlamp near the fork crown—checking each part's coordinates to avoid overlapping the wheel, fender, and bars. I'm now settling on using a single frame joint at the origin with child joints for fork, wheels, and crank (each given appropriate direction/up vectors), and defining helper functions for rods and tubes before writing the wheel-building code.

Writing wheel construction code...

Still laying out the frame geometry...

Now I'm defining the joints for frame, fork, crank, and both wheels, then writing helper functions for rods and mirrored parts, plus assembling the chain, crank arms, spokes, basket, and fender details before finalizing the full bicycle build module.
